slides.title: Converting Length Across Systems; Currency
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: a conversion ratio is a rate too, and it is on the reference sheet. Multiply by it; estimate first.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the move: a ratio, and a division because feet are bigger. A room that writes 360 ft will write 127 in on Notes II. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the ratio and the line.
slides.note: 1 in = 2.54 cm, so 2.54 cm over 1 in is 1 — the top and bottom are the same length in two units. Multiplying by 1 changes nothing but the unit: 10 in × 2.54 cm per in = 25.4 cm, and the inches cancel. The ratio is on the reference sheet; nobody memorises it. **Say:** a conversion is multiplying by a form of 1 — the unit you have cancels, the unit you want is left.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: The sheet gives both directions: 1 in = 2.54 cm and 1 cm = 0.39 in. Pick the one whose 1 is the unit you have, so the unit cancels. 50 cm to inches: a centimetre is shorter than an inch, so there are fewer inches than centimetres — 50 × 0.39 = 19.5 in, never 127. The estimate is what catches the wrong ratio. **Say:** say which answer should be smaller before you touch the calculator.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: An exchange rate is a conversion ratio with a date on it: 0.92 euros per dollar today, something else tomorrow, so it is printed on the problem and never on the sheet. \$150 × 0.92 = 138 euros. Back the other way is a division: 92 euros ÷ 0.92 = \$100. **Say:** the rate is given; the move is the same as inches to centimetres.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask which unit should give the bigger number before anyone multiplies.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 38.1 cm. More centimetres than inches, as the estimate says. A board with 5.9 divided.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.

slides.title: Your Turn

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask what the second question's operation is before anyone writes it.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: 73.60 euros; \$50. The rate is used as a multiplication one way and a division the other. A board with 42.32 for the second part multiplied again.

slides.title: Your Turn

slides.title: Your Turn

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Inches to centimetres, the ratio printed. More centimetres, as the estimate says.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: The same 20, the other way. Fewer inches. A board with 50.8 used board 1's ratio on today's unit. (20 ÷ 2.54 = 7.87 is the sheet's other ratio; accept it.)

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: A new ratio, the same move. A kilometre is shorter, so more of them.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. C is the guide's named misconception — the ratio the wrong way round — and the estimate (a mile is longer, so fewer miles) is the whole answer to it. Sixty seconds and a re-vote on a split.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: A chain: inside customary first, then across. Each step is a form of 1, and the units cancel in order on the paper.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: The boundary board: three conversions, and 3 × 2.54 = 7.62 looks like an answer until the estimate says a table is not 8 cm long. The estimate is not decoration — it is the only thing that catches a wrong chain. Make every board say its estimate first.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The state's own shape (the Assessment Guide's two-hop currency item): two rates, dated and printed, used one after the other. Nobody divides — both hops go forward. A board with 2,640 stopped after the first and multiplied by 10.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): Theo's weight is bait — pounds are Tuesday. The arithmetic is board 4's, now with a number to ignore; a board that converted 110 lb to anything was answering a question nobody asked.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence: the guide's named misconception, caught by the estimate. Both sheet ratios give full credit (11.7 by 0.39, 11.8 by ÷ 2.54); the sentence about direction is what is graded.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
